question: What is the main thing that sets a medical emergency apart from a trauma case?

options.A: It is always caused by a blunt or penetrating external force
options.B: It occurs exclusively in patients with a history of surgery
options.C: It develops slowly over several months without sudden changes
options.D: It arises from internal disease processes or system breakdown

explanation: Think of medical emergencies as coming from within—like an organ failure or sudden illness—while trauma comes from outside forces. You've got this! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h1)

question: Which of these options is a classic example of a traumatic emergency?

options.A: A bone fracture and heavy bleeding following a motor crash
options.B: A sudden stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain
options.C: A severe asthma attack triggered by dust in the ward
options.D: A sudden drop in blood sugar leading to a diabetic coma

explanation: Trauma involves physical force from the outside world, such as a vehicle crash. Great job spotting the difference! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h1)

question: During a community disease outbreak, what is the main cause of biological hazard emergencies?

options.A: Accidental leakage of industrial gas from factories
options.B: Sudden heavy rainfall flooding residential areas
options.C: Rapid spread of infectious diseases among populations
options.D: Widespread consumption of expired tinned foods

explanation: Biological hazards are living microscopic troublemakers like bacteria and viruses that spread fast through communities. Keep up the good work! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h2)

question: A farmer arrives at the clinic with severe muscle twitching and too much saliva after working in the fields. What caused this?

options.A: A natural disaster caused by flooding
options.C: A traumatic injury from a falling tree branch

explanation: Pesticides are powerful chemicals that affect the nervous system, leading to symptoms like twitching and excess saliva. You're learning fast! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the leading cause of severe trauma and head injuries on our roads here in Nigeria?
explanation: Sadly, road traffic accidents are the top reason emergency wards see severe injuries. Stay safe out there! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h3)

question: A child swallowed a brightly colored liquid from a soft drink bottle. What is the nurse's most important first step?

options.A: Place the child flat on their back to rest quietly
options.B: Induce vomiting immediately to remove the liquid
options.C: Identify the exact substance swallowed without delaying care
options.D: Administer large amounts of palm oil to neutralize the poison

explanation: Knowing the exact poison helps the doctor give the right treatment. Never force vomiting for chemicals, as it can cause worse burns on the way back up! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h3)

question: In simple terms, what does cellular hypoxia mean for the body's tissues?

options.A: An excess of sugar circulating in the blood
options.B: A dangerous shortage of oxygen supply
options.C: A sudden increase in total body water volume
options.D: A high concentration of red blood cells

explanation: Hypo means low, and oxia refers to oxygen. It simply means the cells are crying out for the oxygen they need to work! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why does losing a massive amount of blood lead straight into shock?

options.A: The kidneys stop producing urine to save salt and water
options.B: Red blood cells multiply too fast and block small blood vessels
options.C: The heart beats too slowly to pump blood to the lungs
options.D: There is not enough fluid volume to maintain perfusion pressure

explanation: Without enough fluid in the pipes, the blood pressure drops, and vital organs don't get the blood flow they need. You're mastering the core concepts! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which group of people is most at risk of sudden, severe dehydration from diarrhea?
explanation: Little ones have small body reserves and lose water very quickly. That's why childhood diarrhea is treated as an urgent matter! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is a major non-medical challenge that delays emergency survival in many developing areas?

options.A: Strict government regulations on the use of intravenous fluids
options.B: A lack of interest in modern medicine among rural community members
options.C: Delays in reaching a health facility due to financial and transport challenges
options.D: Excessive availability of free ambulance services on major roads

explanation: Transportation bottlenecks and money hurdles often delay patients from getting to the hospital on time. Every minute counts in an emergency! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h5)

question: When doing a quick ABCDE emergency check on a patient, what does the letter 'C' stand for?
explanation: A is Airway, B is Breathing, and C is Circulation! You check pulses and bleeding here. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h6)

question: An unconscious patient is brought to the ward. After checking their airway and breathing, which scale should you use to assess their brain function and alertness?
explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is our trusty bedside tool for checking a patient's level of consciousness. You'll use this a lot in clinicals! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h6)

question: Why do nurses prefer using large-bore IV catheters when handling emergency resuscitation?

options.A: They allow rapid infusion of fluids and emergency drugs
options.B: They can remain inside the vein for up to two weeks safely
options.C: They prevent the need to monitor blood pressure regularly
options.D: They cause less pain when inserted into small arm veins

explanation: A wider tube means fluids can rush in much faster to save a crashing patient. Smart thinking! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the best immediate nursing action for an unconscious patient who is breathing on their own?

options.A: Force fluids by mouth to prevent dehydration during sleep
options.B: Place them in the recovery position to keep the airway clear
options.C: Prop them upright in bed to encourage deep lung breathing
options.D: Tie their arms to the bed rails to prevent sudden movement

explanation: The recovery position keeps the tongue from blocking the airway and lets saliva drain out safely. A classic life-saving nursing skill! [learn more](GNS315_U2_T3#GNS315_U2_T3_h7)
